stories.title: Introducing Hy4 Preview
stories.paragraph: Tencent has released Hy4 Preview, an open-weight text-only large language model with 770 billion total parameters and 49 billion active parameters, using a mixture-of-experts architecture. The model supports a 1 million token context window and weighs 1.56 TB on Hugging Face. This represents a significant size increase over Tencent's previous Hy3 model, released in July, which had 295 billion total parameters, 21 billion active parameters, and a 256,000-token context window. The release adds another large-scale open-weight model to a competitive landscape that includes offerings from Meta and Mistral.

stories.title: Nvidia's AI advantage is moving beyond the GPU
stories.paragraph: Nvidia is expanding its strategic position in the AI market beyond its core GPU hardware business, according to a TechCrunch analysis. The company's CUDA software ecosystem, networking products such as InfiniBand, and enterprise software offerings are increasingly cited as sources of competitive differentiation. This matters because rivals including AMD and Intel have made headway in raw chip performance, making Nvidia's software and systems-level lock-in a key factor in sustaining its market position. The shift signals that Nvidia is positioning itself as a full-stack AI infrastructure provider rather than a semiconductor vendor alone.

stories.title: Meta Project OT plan to replace employees with AI agents
stories.paragraph: Internal communications reported by The Street indicate that Meta has been developing a project, referred to as Project OT, aimed at substituting certain employee roles with AI agents. Mark Zuckerberg has reportedly communicated to staff that AI is expected to take on a growing share of work currently performed by human engineers and other workers. The plan fits into a broader pattern of large technology companies publicly committing to AI-driven workforce restructuring in 2026. Meta has not disclosed the number of roles targeted or a specific timeline for implementation.

stories.title: China is fueling America's data center rage
stories.paragraph: Axios reports that Chinese AI bots and data-scraping activity are a significant driver behind the surge in data center demand that has provoked local opposition across the United States. Communities near large data center developments have increasingly pushed back against the facilities due to their water consumption, energy use, and strain on local power grids. The piece notes that Chinese-origin web traffic is contributing materially to load forecasts that justify new construction, complicating the policy debate around permitting and energy allocation. The dynamic adds a national-security dimension to what had previously been framed largely as an environmental and infrastructure dispute.

stories.title: Fair Work Commission condemns 'plain wrong' AI legal advice
stories.paragraph: Australia's Fair Work Commission has publicly criticized AI-generated legal advice submitted in proceedings, describing it as "plain wrong." The case highlights the risk of litigants or representatives relying on large language model outputs for legal arguments without expert verification. The Commission's condemnation follows similar judicial rebukes in other jurisdictions where AI-produced citations and legal reasoning have been found to be fabricated or materially inaccurate. The incident adds to a growing body of formal institutional pushback against unverified AI use in legal contexts.

stories.title: LLMs are making me lose my savviness
stories.paragraph: A software developer writing on pgaleone.eu argues that regular reliance on large language models is eroding the problem-solving instincts and deep-search habits that practitioners build over years of hands-on work. The author describes noticing a reduced impulse to read documentation carefully or reason through problems independently when an LLM answer is immediately available. The post reflects a concern shared in practitioner communities that productivity gains from AI assistance may come with a less visible cost to individual skill development. The piece does not cite empirical research but draws on the author's own observed behavioral changes over an extended period of LLM use.

stories.title: No AI Fridays
stories.paragraph: The website No AI Fridays proposes a structured practice of abstaining from AI tool use one day per week, framing it as a way for practitioners to maintain independent problem-solving skills. The initiative positions itself as a personal discipline rather than a political campaign, suggesting that a regular AI-free day can help professionals stay aware of their own capabilities and dependencies. The site does not present quantitative evidence for its claims but aligns with growing discourse around cognitive offloading and skill atrophy among AI-tool users. It joins a small number of similar individual-practice movements that have emerged as daily AI use has become routine in technical workplaces.

stories.title: The elementary school pickup incident and the road ahead
stories.paragraph: A post on shitposting.ai recounts a specific incident in which an AI-related misunderstanding or failure caused a real-world problem at an elementary school pickup, using it as a lens to discuss broader concerns about AI systems operating in everyday social contexts. The piece argues that the gap between AI capability demonstrations and reliable, safe deployment in unstructured real-world situations remains substantial. The author uses the anecdote to question the pace at which AI tools are being integrated into contexts involving children and logistical coordination. No specific system or company is named as responsible for the incident described.

stories.title: Smartphone LED Detects Hidden Cameras with AI
stories.paragraph: Researchers have developed a technique that uses a smartphone's LED flash and an AI model to detect hidden cameras in a room, according to a report in the Chosun Ilbo. The method works by analyzing the reflective signatures of camera lenses when illuminated by the LED, with an AI classifier distinguishing camera optics from other reflective surfaces. Hidden camera detection has become a pressing concern in South Korea, where illicit recording cases have been widely reported. The approach requires only a standard smartphone, lowering the barrier to access compared with dedicated detection hardware.

stories.title: Show HN: AI Agents for Osint/Sigint
stories.paragraph: Makra Labs has released an early prototype of an AI agent system designed for open-source intelligence and signals intelligence tasks, reducing context engineering costs through a technique the developers call Layout Memoization. Rather than passing full HTML into the context window, the system uses a continual-learning browser harness that extracts structured or tabular data from publicly accessible web pages. The tool can spin up a browser instance and retrieve information from arbitrary open-web sources in a read-only mode. The project is positioned as a cost-reduction approach for context-heavy web-crawling agent workflows.

stories.title: Open Oscar Server: open-source server compatible with AIM and ICQ clients
stories.paragraph: Developer mk6i has published Open Oscar Server, an open-source implementation of the OSCAR protocol used by AOL Instant Messenger and ICQ, allowing vintage clients from the late 1990s and 2000s to connect to a self-hosted server. The project enables users to run a private instant messaging environment compatible with original AIM and ICQ software without relying on AOL's now-defunct infrastructure. OSCAR, which stood for Open System for Communication in Realtime, was the proprietary protocol that underpinned both services at their peak of popularity. The repository is hosted on GitHub and accepts contributions, making it part of a small but active community preserving legacy internet communication protocols.

stories.title: The Internet Archive's Vintage AI Collection
stories.paragraph: The Internet Archive has assembled a Vintage AI Collection, gathering historical software, papers, and media related to artificial intelligence research and applications from earlier decades. The collection provides public access to artifacts that document the field's development prior to the current deep-learning era, including materials from symbolic AI and expert systems periods. Preserving this material is notable because many early AI programs and publications were not widely digitized, making them difficult to access for historical research. The archive's collection is browsable online and freely accessible without registration.

stories.title: Good Culture Is the Biggest Productivity Hack, Not AI
stories.paragraph: An engineering leadership newsletter argues that organizational culture has a larger effect on team productivity than AI tooling. The piece contends that psychological safety, clear communication, and trust between engineers and management drive output more reliably than adopting the latest AI-assisted development tools. The argument is notable as it pushes back against the prevailing narrative in the tech industry that AI adoption is the primary lever for engineering efficiency gains.

stories.title: The growing divide between AI hype and software engineering reality
stories.paragraph: A post on Optimized by Otto examines why a number of open-source projects have introduced explicit bans or restrictions on AI-generated code contributions. The piece highlights a gap between vendor claims about AI coding tools and the practical quality concerns — such as subtle bugs, license ambiguity, and increased review burden — that open-source maintainers report encountering. The trend of formal AI contribution policies in open-source communities represents a concrete, measurable response to questions about code provenance and maintainability that broader industry discourse has largely glossed over.
